  echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  comment = "#>", collapse = TRUE,

**A team that scores 110 points per 100 possessions against the best defenses in
the country is better than one that does it against the weakest. Opponent-adjusted
ratings correct for that, so every Division I women's team sits on one scale
regardless of schedule.** `load_wbb_ratings()` returns, for each team and season,
adjusted offensive and defensive efficiency (points scored and allowed per 100
possessions against an average opponent), adjusted tempo, and the adjusted
efficiency margin, the difference between the two.

This article explains what the ratings measure, how they are computed, how they
are checked, and their known issues. It condenses the official model card in the
[wehoop-wbb-data repository](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/wehoop-wbb-data/blob/main/docs/models/ratings.md);
numbers quoted from that card are labelled as such.

## What the model estimates

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `adj_o` | Adjusted offensive efficiency: points scored per 100 possessions against an average defense |
| `adj_d` | Adjusted defensive efficiency: points allowed per 100 possessions against an average offense (lower is better) |
| `adj_em` | Adjusted efficiency margin, `adj_o - adj_d` |
| `adj_em_z` | `adj_em` as a z-score within the season |
| `adj_tempo` | Adjusted possessions per 40 minutes |
| `raw_o`, `raw_d` | Unadjusted points scored and allowed per 100 possessions |
| `games`, `rank` | Games in the fit and national rank by `adj_em` |

The design is the same family as the KenPom and Bart Torvik ratings that are
standard in college basketball analysis.

## Loading the ratings

```{r libraries}
library(wehoop)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

The ratings are published as Parquet files, so `load_wbb_ratings()` needs the
`arrow` package.

```{r load}
ratings <- load_wbb_ratings(seasons = 2026)

nrow(ratings)
```

The ratings carry ESPN team ids. Team names come from the box scores; cast both
id columns to character so the join cannot silently fail on an integer-versus-
character mismatch.

```{r names}
team_names <- load_wbb_team_box(seasons = 2026) |>
  transmute(team_id = as.character(team_id), team = team_location) |>
  distinct(team_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

ratings <- ratings |>
  mutate(team_id = as.character(team_id)) |>
  left_join(team_names, by = "team_id")

ratings |>
  arrange(rank) |>
  select(rank, team, games, adj_o, adj_d, adj_em, adj_tempo) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 1))) |>
  print(n = 25)
```

## Data

As reported in the model card, the ratings are computed from this season's
published women's college play-by-play and box scores, the same files
`load_wbb_pbp()` and `load_wbb_team_box()` read. They are recomputed from scratch
on every run rather than updated incrementally, so a correction to the underlying
data flows through on the next publish.

The full table includes every opponent a Division I team played, including
non-Division I teams with only a game or two. Those teams pull the overall mean
far below zero, so most analysis should use the core of teams with a full
schedule. The model card uses 10 or more games.

```{r core}
core <- ratings |> filter(games >= 10)

c(all_teams = nrow(ratings), core_teams = nrow(core))
```

## How the model works

Raw efficiency is points per 100 possessions. Adjustment asks how a team would
have done against an average opponent. A team's adjusted offense depends on how
good the defenses it faced were, and those defenses' adjusted ratings depend on
the offenses they faced, so the ratings are solved together: start from raw
efficiency, adjust every team for its opponents, and repeat until the numbers
stop changing (a fixed point). As reported in the model card, the engine is the
sportsdataverse-py women's college prediction stack's iterative opponent
adjustment.

The model has no hidden machinery: its inputs are the game results, its output
is the offense and defense split, and its main check is external agreement with
reference rating systems.

```{r surface, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of 2025-26 NCAA women's teams with at least 10 games: adjusted offensive efficiency against adjusted defensive efficiency, defense axis reversed."}
ggplot(core, aes(adj_o, adj_d)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#7c689c") +
  geom_text(aes(label = team), data = core |> filter(rank <= 8),
            size = 3, vjust = -0.8, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    title = "2025-26 women's college basketball: the rating surface",
    subtitle = "Teams with 10+ games. Up and to the right is better.",
    x = "Adjusted offense (points per 100)", y = "Adjusted defense (reversed)",
    caption = "Data: wehoop::load_wbb_ratings()"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## How well does it work?

### Internal consistency

```{r consistency}
core |>
  summarise(
    mean_adj_em = mean(adj_em),
    cor_adj_em_vs_raw_margin = cor(adj_em, raw_o - raw_d),
    cor_adj_em_vs_z = cor(adj_em, adj_em_z)
  )
```

The core's mean should sit near zero, and the adjusted margin should correlate
strongly but not perfectly with the raw margin. The gap below 1 is the schedule
effect the model exists to remove: mid-major teams with large raw margins move
down, and power-conference teams with hard schedules move up.

### Does the adjusted margin explain game results better than the raw one?

For every 2025-26 game between two core teams, compare the home team's actual
margin with the difference in the two teams' ratings. This is an in-sample check,
because the season-end ratings were computed from these same games, but it shows
what the adjustment adds over raw margins.

```{r margins}
wbb_box <- load_wbb_team_box(seasons = 2026) |>
  filter(team_home_away == "home") |>
  transmute(
    home_id = as.character(team_id), away_id = as.character(opponent_team_id),
    margin = team_score - opponent_team_score
  )

core_ids <- core |> transmute(team_id, adj_em, raw_margin = raw_o - raw_d)

games <- wbb_box |>
  inner_join(rename_with(core_ids, ~ paste0("home_", .x)), by = c(home_id = "home_team_id")) |>
  inner_join(rename_with(core_ids, ~ paste0("away_", .x)), by = c(away_id = "away_team_id"))

games |>
  summarise(
    games = n(),
    cor_adjusted = cor(margin, home_adj_em - away_adj_em),
    cor_raw = cor(margin, home_raw_margin - away_raw_margin)
  )
```

### Program stability across seasons

Programs persist even though rosters turn over. The year-over-year correlation of
a team's adjusted margin:

```{r yoy}
prior <- load_wbb_ratings(seasons = 2025) |>
  filter(games >= 10) |>
  transmute(team_id = as.character(team_id), adj_em_2025 = adj_em)

core |>
  inner_join(prior, by = "team_id") |>
  summarise(teams = n(), yoy_correlation = cor(adj_em, adj_em_2025))
```

### The level gate

A rank correlation against another rating system cannot see a scale error:
multiply every rating by 100 and the ranks do not move. As reported in the model
card, the publish path therefore also checks absolute levels over the core
teams: mean `adj_o` in [85, 105], mean `adj_d` in [80, 100], mean `adj_em` in
[-12, 12], mean `adj_tempo` in [64, 78], and the spread (standard deviation) of
`adj_em` in [14, 28], with no non-finite values. The gate applies once at least
150 teams have 10 or more games. Re-running it on the 2026 release:

```{r level-gate}
core |>
  summarise(
    core_teams = n(),
    non_finite = sum(!is.finite(adj_em)),
    mean_adj_o = mean(adj_o), mean_adj_d = mean(adj_d),
    mean_adj_em = mean(adj_em), mean_adj_tempo = mean(adj_tempo),
    sd_adj_em = sd(adj_em)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    passes = core_teams >= 150 & non_finite == 0 &
      between(mean_adj_o, 85, 105) & between(mean_adj_d, 80, 100) &
      between(mean_adj_em, -12, 12) & between(mean_adj_tempo, 64, 78) &
      between(sd_adj_em, 14, 28)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "check", values_to = "value",
                      values_transform = as.character)
```

## Reproducing it yourself

- Ratings: `load_wbb_ratings(seasons = ...)` (needs `arrow`).
- Inputs: `load_wbb_team_box()` and `load_wbb_pbp()` for the same season.
- Raw ratings by hand: the [advanced metrics article](womens-basketball-advanced-metrics.html#womens-college-basketball)
  computes the unadjusted version from box scores.
- Method and evaluation in full: the
  [model card](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/wehoop-wbb-data/blob/main/docs/models/ratings.md).

## Limitations and known issues

As reported in the model card:

- **2015 is missing.** The published 2015 file has no usable ratings (the fixed
  point did not converge on that season's inputs), which also leaves the 2015
  player value file empty. A repair and republish is pending.
- **Older seasons are thin.** Seasons before about 2017 have fewer teams with a
  full schedule in the box scores, and seasons before 2013 sit on a different
  possession scale because of the older box score format. The 2008 file fails the
  level gate. Use pre-2017 ratings with care.
- **No preseason prior.** Early-season ratings start from a flat slate, so they
  are noisy until teams have played enough games.
- **Home court and travel.** Altitude and travel distance are not modelled.
